attribution: Tiruvalluvar, about whom little is known with certainty
author: tiruvalluvar
period: Scholars place it variously between roughly the 1st century BCE and the 6th century CE; many favour the middle of the first millennium CE
summary: A Tamil classic of 1330 two-line couplets on virtue, wealth and love, among the most admired works of ethical literature in India.
whyRead: It offers practical, humane ethics for everyday and public life, without sectarian commitment, which is why many religious traditions have claimed it. Its couplets are short and memorable.
questions: How should one live well in the world?
What makes a good ruler, friend or spouse?

keyTeachings.title: Virtue (Aram)
keyTeachings.text: The first book treats household and ascetic virtue: kindness, truthfulness, gratitude, patience, non-violence and the avoidance of meat and envy.

keyTeachings.title: Wealth and governance (Porul)
keyTeachings.text: The second and longest book covers kingship, ministers, statecraft, friendship and the proper acquisition and use of wealth.

keyTeachings.title: Love (Inbam)
keyTeachings.text: The third book treats love in the manner of classical Tamil poetry, through the phases of love in secret and married love.

keyTeachings.title: Broadly non-sectarian
keyTeachings.text: The text praises the divine in its opening chapter but avoids naming a particular deity or school; Jain, Shaiva and other traditions have each claimed it.

structure.label: Three books
structure.note: Aram (virtue, 38 chapters), Porul (wealth, 70 chapters), Inbam (love, 25 chapters)

passages.about: The opening couplet in praise of the divine
